performers: Pierre Bernac, baritone; Francis Poulenc, piano
intro: The last three songs of Poulenc’s nine-song Éluard cycle Tel jour telle nuit fill the third side of HMV DB 6383–6384. Pierre Bernac sings and the composer plays; the set was listed for sale as an import by March 1948.

sections.label: A · Je n’ai envie que de t’aimer
B · Figure de force brûlante et farouche
C · Nous avons fait la nuit

cues.title: Songs 7–9 of nine
cues.text: This side carries the last three of the nine songs. Poulenc composed the first and last songs of the cycle together, as a matching pair, in Lyon, after beginning the work at Noizay in December 1936.
cues.evidence: Graham Johnson, note on Tel jour telle nuit, FP 86, Hyperion CDH55366, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4310_66147: begun in December 1936 at Noizay and completed by January 1937, with “the first and last songs composed as a matching pair in Lyon”. The contents of the side are listed in the Internet Archive item for DB 6384: https://archive.org/details/78_tel-jour-telle-nuit-no-3_pierre-bernac-francis-poulenc-poulenc_gbia0553972a

cues.title: The dedicatees
cues.text: Poulenc dedicated the songs of the cycle to eight people, among them Picasso, Nusch Éluard, Valentine Hugo, the baritone Pierre Bernac and the choral conductor Yvonne Gouverné.
cues.evidence: Graham Johnson, note on Tel jour telle nuit, FP 86, Hyperion CDH55366, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4310_66147: the dedicatees named are Picasso, Freddy (Fréderique Lebedeff), Nusch Éluard, Valentine Hugo, Marie-Blanche de Polignac, Denise Bourdet, Pierre Bernac and Yvonne Gouverné.

cues.title: Song 9, the last of the cycle
cues.text: The ninth song, “Nous avons fait la nuit”, closes the cycle. Graham Johnson calls the last song of the cycle a summing-up of what has gone before.
cues.evidence: Graham Johnson, note on Tel jour telle nuit, FP 86, Hyperion CDH55366, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4310_66147: “the last song a summing-up of what has gone before”.

cues.title: “Je ris encore”
cues.text: John Check singles out the phrase “Je ris encore” in this song, where a bold ascending leap on the second word captures the exhilaration of the phrase.
cues.evidence: John Check, review of Roger Nichols, Poulenc: A Biography, The New Criterion, 21 May 2020, https://newcriterion.com/dispatch/poulencs-voice/: the leap on the second word of “Je ris encore” in “Nous avons fait la nuit”. The words are sung about 2:45 into this track.

cues.title: Éluard’s four titles
cues.text: In early January 1937, with the first performance a month away, Poulenc asked Éluard for a title. Éluard offered four; his own choice was Tout dire, and Poulenc took the second, Tel jour telle nuit.
cues.evidence: Graham Johnson, note on Tel jour telle nuit, FP 86, Hyperion CDH55366, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4310_66147: Poulenc asked the poet for a title; Éluard preferred Tout dire and Poulenc chose his second suggestion, Tel jour telle nuit.

cues.title: Piano postlude
cues.text: After the last words, “toujours nouveau”, the piano plays a postlude in a new tonality. Check finds it Schubert-like in its breadth and says it sums up the cycle as a whole.
cues.evidence: John Check, review of Roger Nichols, Poulenc: A Biography, The New Criterion, 21 May 2020, https://newcriterion.com/dispatch/poulencs-voice/: the final words “toujours nouveau” “open to a piano postlude in a new tonality, Schubert-like in its breadth, that encapsulates the cycle as a whole”.

cues.title: The record in March 1948
cues.text: The Gramophone Shop’s supplement for March 1948 listed this set, the cycle on three sides and Dans le jardin d’Anna on a fourth. It wrote that the performances “may be considered authentic, by virtue of the composer’s participation in the recording”.
cues.evidence: The Gramophone Shop Supplement, March 1948 (Internet Archive), https://archive.org/details/gramophone-shop-supplement-1948-03: the entry for G-DB6383/4, two 12-inch imported records priced at $5.24.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Internet Archive item credits Pierre Bernac and Francis Poulenc and lists baritone and piano; the March 1948 supplement names both and cites “the composer’s participation in the recording”.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Songs 7, 8 and 9 of the nine-song cycle for voice and piano, on the third side of the set.
fields.note: The Internet Archive item lists the three songs on this side in this order. The dealer’s supplement lists the nine songs and says the cycle occupies three sides. The printed edition used is not named.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The set was listed as an import by March 1948. The Internet Archive metadata for the other two sides of the set gives “1948-12”, which is later than that listing and so cannot be the date of recording or first issue.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The supplement lists two 12-inch imported records, Nos. G-DB6383/4.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: DB 6384, side 1 (the cycle’s first six songs are on the two sides of DB 6383)
fields.note: The Internet Archive label data read “D.B.6384” for this side, with Dans le jardin d’Anna on the other; the other transfers of the set read “D.B.6383”.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: 2EA 11110-1 (this side); the reverse, Dans le jardin d’Anna, is 2EA 11131
fields.note: From the item descriptions of the two transfers.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: George Blood, L.P., for the Great 78 Project (Internet Archive); disc from the Goodfriend collection
fields.note: The item description names the engineer’s firm and lists the collections georgeblood and 78rpm_goodfriend.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.value: Not stated; the item was made public on 1 July 2024
fields.note: The public date of the item is an upload date, not the date of the transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Four stylus sizes were tried; the preferred version was equalised with turnover 375 Hz and roll-off −12 dB, and copied under the friendlier file name.
fields.note: As stated in the item description. The published MP3 is the Internet Archive derivative of that file.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Poulenc died in 1963, so the music is in copyright in the EU under the life-plus-70 term, which runs to the end of 2033; national wartime extensions, which can lengthen the term for older works in France, were not assessed. The poems are by Paul Éluard, who died in 1952; rights in the poems are not assessed here.
fields.note: Rights in the composition are stated separately from rights in the recording. The dates of death are those given in the cited note; the United States status of the music and the poems is not established here.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963; listed as an import by March 1948.
fields.note: The United States status of a recording made in France in the 1940s is not established.

composer.epithet: Pianist and composer of sacred works, love songs and an opera in which the choir is silenced by the guillotine.
facts: Piano with Ricardo Viñes; counterpoint and composition with Charles Koechlin
Georges Auric · Jean Cocteau · Guillaume Apollinaire · Paul Éluard
Pierre Bernac, baritone; Denise Duval, soprano; Poulenc at the piano
Three operas, songs, choral music, ballets, concertos and wind sonatas
composer.background:
Ricardo Viñes used his feet as well as his hands when he taught the piano. When his pupil Francis Poulenc mishandled the pedal, a buttoned boot prodded his shin. Poulenc remembered the lessons with affection: “I owe him everything,” he told Claude Rostand in their radio conversations of 1953–54. Viñes taught him to make a staccato note sing through the pedal and to distinguish sharply between kinds of touch. Poulenc later adopted his own remedy, in the language of the kitchen, for a meagre piano sound: “Put butter in the sauce!”

He was born in Paris on 7 January 1899. His father Émile ran a chemical business; his mother Jenny came from a family of Parisian artisans and began teaching him piano when he was five. She played Mozart and Schubert, Chopin and salon pieces. Poulenc’s tastes included what he later called “adorable bad music”. His uncle Marcel Royer, known as Papoum, took him to concerts and the theatre. Through the Ballets Russes he came to know Stravinsky, and Debussy’s scores were always in the house. “It is my oxygen,” he told Rostand of Debussy’s music.
